subject: Polity
concepts: Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12 to 35) – Fundamental Rights
Inspiration from the Constitution of USA (Bill of Rights)
Magna Carta of India
Justiciable Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights more elaborate than any other country including USA
Fundamental Rights guaranteed without discrimination
Upholding equality of all individuals
Upholding dignity of the individual
Upholding larger public interest
Upholding unity of the nation
Promoting political democracy
Preventing authoritarian and despotic rule
Protecting liberties against invasion by the State
Limitations on tyranny of executive
Limitations on arbitrary laws of legislature
Government of laws and not of men
Fundamental law of the land
All-round development (material, intellectual, moral, spiritual)
Originally seven Fundamental Rights
Right to equality (Articles 14–18)
Right to freedom (Articles 19–22)
Right against exploitation (Articles 23–24)
Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25–28)
Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29–30)
Right to property (Article 31)
Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32)
Deletion of right to property from Fundamental Rights
44th Amendment Act, 1978
Right to property as legal right under Article 300-A in Part XII
At present only six Fundamental Rights
Features of Fundamental Rights
Some rights available only to citizens, others to all persons (citizens, foreigners, legal persons)
Fundamental Rights not absolute but qualified
State can impose reasonable restrictions
Courts decide whether restrictions are reasonable
Balance between individual rights and society, liberty and social control
Rights available against arbitrary action of state
Some rights also available against private individuals
Some rights negative (limitations on State), some positive (conferring privileges)
Justiciable – persons can move courts for enforcement
Defended and guaranteed by Supreme Court
Aggrieved person can directly go to Supreme Court not necessarily by appeal
Fundamental Rights not sacrosanct or permanent
Parliament can curtail or repeal by constitutional amendment, not ordinary act
Cannot affect ‘basic structure’ of Constitution
Amenability of fundamental rights (Chapter 11)
Suspension during National Emergency except Articles 20 and 21
Suspension of Article 19 rights only during external emergency (war or external aggression), not internal emergency (armed rebellion)
Suspension of fundamental rights during national emergency (Chapter 16)
Scope limited by Article 31A (saving of laws for acquisition of estates, etc.)
Article 31B (validation of acts and regulations in Ninth Schedule)
Article 31C (saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles)
Application to armed forces, para-military, police, intelligence agencies can be restricted or abrogated by Parliament (Article 33)
Application can be restricted while martial law in force (Article 34)
Martial law – military rule under abnormal circumstances to restore order
Difference between martial law and national emergency
Most fundamental rights directly enforceable (self-executory)
Some enforced on basis of law made by Parliament (not state legislatures) – Article 35
Definition of State – Article 12
State includes Government and Parliament of India (executive and legislative organs of Union)
Government and legislature of states (executive and legislative organs of state governments)
All local authorities (municipalities, panchayats, district boards, improvement trusts)
All other authorities (statutory or non-statutory like LIC, ONGC, SAIL)
State defined in wider sense including all agencies
Actions of State agencies can be challenged in courts as violating Fundamental Rights
Supreme Court: private body or agency working as instrument of State falls within meaning of State under Article 12
Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights – Article 13
All laws inconsistent with or in derogation of fundamental rights shall be void
Doctrine of judicial review
Power of Supreme Court (Article 32) and high courts (Article 226) to declare law unconstitutional
Term ‘law’ in Article 13 – wide connotation
Permanent laws enacted by Parliament or state legislatures
Temporary laws like ordinances issued by President or state governors
Statutory instruments (delegated legislation) – order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification
Non-legislative sources – custom or usage having force of law
Constitutional amendment is not a law and cannot be challenged normally
Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) – constitutional amendment can be challenged if it violates a fundamental right forming part of basic structure
Table 7.1 – Fundamental Rights at a Glance
Right to equality (Articles 14–18)
Equality before law and equal protection of laws (Article 14)
Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15)
Equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16)
Abolition of untouchability (Article 17)
Abolition of titles except military and academic (Article 18)
Right to freedom (Articles 19–22)
Protection of six rights regarding freedom: speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession (Article 19)
Protection in respect of conviction for offences (Article 20)
Protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21)
Right to elementary education (Article 21A)
Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases (Article 22)
Right against exploitation (Articles 23–24)
Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour (Article 23)
Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc. (Article 24)
Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25–28)
Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion (Article 25)
Freedom to manage religious affairs (Article 26)
Freedom from payment of taxes for promotion of any religion (Article 27)
Freedom from attending religious instruction or worship in certain educational institutions (Article 28)
Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29–30)
Protection of language, script and culture of minorities (Article 29)
Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions (Article 30)
Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32)
Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights including writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto
Table 7.2 – Fundamental Rights of Foreigners
FR available only to citizens: Articles 15, 16, 19, 21, 30
FR available to both citizens and foreigners (except enemy aliens): Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28
Right to Equality – Article 14
Equality before law – British origin
Equal protection of laws – American Constitution
Concept of equality before law: absence of special privileges, equal subjection to ordinary law, no person above law
Concept of equal protection of laws: equality of treatment under equal circumstances, similar application of same laws to similarly situated persons, like should be treated alike
Negative concept (equality before law) vs positive concept (equal protection of laws)
Both aim at equality of legal status, opportunity and justice
Supreme Court: where equals and unequals treated differently, Article 14 does not apply
Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification
Classification should not be arbitrary, artificial or evasive; based on intelligible differentia and substantial distinction
Rule of Law – concept of A.V. Dicey
Three elements of Dicey’s Rule of Law: absence of arbitrary power, equality before law, primacy of rights of individual
First and second elements applicable to Indian System, not third
In Indian System, constitution is source of individual rights
Supreme Court: Rule of Law as embodied in Article 14 is a basic feature of Constitution
Exceptions to equality before law
Immunities of President of India and Governor of States (Article 361)
President/Governor not answerable to court for exercise of powers and duties
No criminal proceedings against President/Governor during term of office
No process for arrest or imprisonment of President/Governor during term
No civil proceedings against President/Governor during term until two months after notice
Immunity for publication of substantially true report of parliamentary/state legislature proceedings (Article 361-A)
Immunity of MPs for anything said or vote given in Parliament or committees (Article 105)
Immunity of MLAs for anything said or vote given in Legislature or committees (Article 194)
Article 31C as exception to Article 14 – laws implementing Directive Principles of Article 39(b) or (c) cannot be challenged for violating Article 14
Supreme Court: where Article 31C comes in, Article 14 goes out
Immunity of foreign sovereigns, ambassadors, diplomats from criminal and civil proceedings
Immunity of UNO and its agencies
Prohibition of Discrimination on Certain Grounds – Article 15
State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Word ‘discrimination’ means to make adverse distinction
Word ‘only’ means discrimination on other grounds not prohibited

Second provision of Article 15: no citizen shall be subjected to disability on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth regarding access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment; use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, places of public resort maintained by State funds or dedicated to public use
This prohibition applies to both State and private individuals (first provision only against State)
Four exceptions to non-discrimination under Article 15
Exception (a): State can make special provision for women and children (e.g., reservation in local bodies, free education for children)
Exception (b): State can make special provision for socially and educationally backward classes or SCs and STs (e.g., reservation in public educational institutions)

Exception (c): State can make special provision for advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes or SCs/STs regarding admission to educational institutions including private (aided or unaided) except minority institutions – added by 93rd Amendment Act, 2005

Exception (d): State can make special provision for economically weaker sections (EWS) including reservation of up to 10% seats in educational institutions (including private aided/unaided except minority institutions) – added by 103rd Amendment Act, 2019
EWS reservation is in addition to existing reservations
EWS to be notified by state on basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage
Reservation for OBCs in Educational Institutions
93rd Amendment Act of 2005
Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006 – 27% quota for OBCs in central higher educational institutions including IITs and IIMs
April 2008 – Supreme Court upheld validity of Amendment Act and OBC Quota Act
Supreme Court directed exclusion of ‘creamy layer’ among OBCs
Creamy layer among OBCs: persons holding constitutional posts (President, VP, Judges, UPSC/SPSC members, CEC, CAG, etc.)
Group A/Class I and Group B/Class II officers of All India, Central and State Services; equivalent in PSUs, Banks, Insurance, Universities, private employment
Persons of rank colonel and above in Army, equivalent in Navy, Air Force, Paramilitary
Professionals like doctors, lawyers, engineers, artists, authors, consultants
Persons engaged in trade, business, industry
People holding agricultural land above certain limit or vacant land/buildings in urban areas
Persons with gross annual income more than ₹8 lakh or possessing wealth above exemption limit
Evolution of creamy layer income ceiling: ₹1 lakh (1993), ₹2.5 lakh (2004), ₹4.5 lakh (2008), ₹6 lakh (2013), ₹8 lakh (2017)
Reservation for EWSs in Educational Institutions – 103rd Amendment Act, 2019
Central government order (2019) providing 10% reservation to EWSs in admission to educational institutions
EWS benefit for persons not covered under existing SC, ST, OBC reservations
Eligibility criteria for EWS: family gross annual income below ₹8 lakh from all sources (salary, agriculture, business, profession) for financial year prior to year of application

Exclusion from EWS if family owns: 5 acres agricultural land and above; residential flat 1000 sq.ft. and above; residential plot 100 sq.yards and above in notified municipalities; residential plot 200 sq.yards and above in other areas
Property held by family in different locations clubbed
Family includes person seeking benefit, parents, siblings below 18, spouse, children below 18
Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment – Article 16
Equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters of employment or appointment under State
No discrimination on grounds of only religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence
Four exceptions to Article 16

Exception (a): Parliament can prescribe residence as condition for certain employment in state/UT/local/other authority – Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act of 1957 expired in 1974; now only Andhra Pradesh (Article 371D) and Telangana (extended by Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014)
Exception (b): State can provide reservation for any backward class not adequately represented in state services
Exception (c): Law can provide that incumbent of office related to religious or denominational institution or its governing body should belong to particular religion or denomination
Exception (d): State can make provision for reservation of up to 10% appointments/posts for economically weaker sections – added by 103rd Amendment Act, 2019
EWS reservation in public employment: central government order (2019) providing 10% reservation in civil posts and services of Government of India

Scientific and technical posts can be exempted from EWS reservation if: posts above lower grade in Group A; classified as scientific/technical per Cabinet Secretariat Order (1961); posts for conducting/organizing/guiding/directing research
Mandal Commission and Aftermath
Second Backward Classes Commission appointed in 1979 by Morarji Desai Government under chairmanship of B.P. Mandal (MP) – under Article 340
Commission submitted report in 1980
Identified 3743 castes as socially and educationally backward classes
They constitute nearly 52% of population (excluding SCs and STs)
Commission recommended 27% reservation in government jobs for OBCs so total reservation (SCs, STs, OBCs) = 50%
1990 – V.P. Singh Government declared 27% reservation for OBCs

1991 – Narasimha Rao Government introduced: (a) preference to poorer sections among OBCs in 27% quota (economic criteria); (b) reservation of another 10% for poorer sections of higher castes not covered by existing reservations
Mandal case (Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, 1992)
Supreme Court examined scope of Article 16(4)
Court rejected additional 10% reservation for poorer higher castes
Upheld constitutional validity of 27% reservation for OBCs with conditions

Conditions: (a) exclude creamy layer among OBCs; (b) no reservation in promotions, confine to initial appointments; existing promotion reservation can continue for five years (upto 1997); (c) total reserved quota should not exceed 50% except extraordinary situations; (d) carry forward rule for backlog vacancies valid but not violate 50% rule; (e) permanent statutory body to examine complaints of over-inclusion and under-inclusion in OBC list
Government actions after Mandal case
Ram Nandan Committee appointed to identify creamy layer among OBCs – submitted report in 1993, accepted
National Commission for Backward Classes established in 1993 by act of Parliament – mandate to examine complaints of under-inclusion, over-inclusion, non-inclusion for job reservation
102nd Amendment Act of 2018 conferred constitutional status on commission and enlarged functions – inserted new Article 338-B
77th Amendment Act (1995) added new provision in Article 16 empowering State to provide reservation in promotions for SCs and STs not adequately represented
85th Amendment Act (2001) provides for ‘consequential seniority’ in promotion by virtue of reservation for SCs/STs with retrospective effect from June 1995

81st Amendment Act (2000) added another new provision in Article 16 empowering State to consider unfilled reserved vacancies of a year as separate class not to be combined with current year vacancies for 50% ceiling – ends 50% ceiling on backlog vacancies
76th Amendment Act (1994) placed Tamil Nadu Reservations Act (1994) in Ninth Schedule to protect it from judicial review (69% reservation far exceeding 50% ceiling)
Abolition of Untouchability – Article 17
Article 17 abolishes ‘untouchability’ and forbids its practice in any form
Enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability is an offence punishable by law
Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 – comprehensively amended and renamed as Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 in 1976
Act defines civil right as any right accruing by reason of abolition of untouchability under Article 17
Term ‘untouchability’ not defined in Constitution or Act

Mysore High Court: subject matter is not literal untouchability but practice as developed historically – social disabilities imposed on certain classes by birth in certain castes; does not cover social boycott of few individuals or exclusion from religious services
Supreme Court: right under Article 17 available against private individuals; State has constitutional obligation to ensure this right not violated
Abolition of Titles – Article 18
Article 18 prohibits state from conferring any title (except military or academic distinction) on any person (citizen or foreigner)
Prohibits citizen from accepting any title from foreign state
Foreigner holding office of profit or trust under State cannot accept title from foreign state without President’s consent
No citizen or foreigner holding office of profit or trust under State to accept any present, emolument or office from foreign state without President’s consent
Hereditary titles of nobility (Maharaja, Raj Bahadur, etc.) banned as against principle of equal status

1996 – Supreme Court upheld constitutional validity of National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Sri) – not ‘titles’ under Article 18 (only hereditary titles of nobility prohibited)
National Awards should not be used as suffixes or prefixes – otherwise forfeited
National Awards instituted in 1954
Janata Party government (Morarji Desai) discontinued them in 1977
Revived in 1980 by Indira Gandhi government
Right to Freedom – Article 19
Six rights guaranteed to all citizens under Article 19
Right to freedom of speech and expression
Right to assemble peaceably and without arms
Right to form associations or unions or co-operative societies
Right to move freely throughout territory of India
Right to reside and settle in any part of territory of India
Right to practice any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business
Originally seven rights – right to acquire, hold and dispose of property deleted by 44th Amendment Act, 1978
These six rights protected against state action only, not private individuals
Available only to citizens and shareholders of a company, not foreigners or legal persons
State can impose ‘reasonable’ restrictions only on grounds mentioned in Article 19 itself

Freedom of Speech and Expression – includes: right to propagate own and others’ views; freedom of press; freedom of commercial advertisements; right against tapping of telephonic conversation; right to telecast (government has no monopoly on electronic media); right against bundh called by political party; right to know about government activities; freedom of silence; right against imposition of pre-censorship on newspaper; right to demonstration or picketing but not right to strike

Reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech and expression on grounds: sovereignty and integrity of India, security of state, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence

Freedom of Assembly – right to hold public meetings, demonstrations, take out processions; can be exercised only on public land; must be peaceful and unarmed; does not protect violent, disorderly, riotous assemblies or those involving arms; does not include right to strike
Reasonable restrictions on assembly on grounds: sovereignty and integrity of India, public order (including maintenance of traffic)

Section 144 of Criminal Procedure Code (1973) – magistrate can restrain assembly, meeting or procession if risk of obstruction, annoyance, danger to life/health/safety, disturbance of public tranquillity, riot or affray

Section 141 of Indian Penal Code – assembly of five or more persons becomes unlawful if object is to resist execution of law/legal process, forcibly occupy property, commit mischief/criminal trespass, force person to do illegal act, threaten government/officials exercising lawful powers

Freedom of Association – right to form political parties, companies, partnership firms, societies, clubs, organisations, trade unions, any body of persons; includes right to start and continue association; covers negative right not to form or join; reasonable restrictions on grounds of sovereignty and integrity of India, public order, morality
Right to obtain recognition of association is not a fundamental right
Supreme Court: trade unions have no guaranteed right to effective bargaining, strike or lock-out; right to strike can be controlled by industrial law

Freedom of Movement – entitles every citizen to move freely throughout country (from one state to another or within state); promotes national feeling; reasonable restrictions on grounds of interests of general public and protection of interests of any scheduled tribe; entry of outsiders in tribal areas restricted to protect tribal culture, language, customs, traditional vocation and properties
Supreme Court: freedom of movement of prostitutes can be restricted on ground of public health and public morals; Bombay High Court validated restrictions on movement of persons affected by AIDS
Two dimensions of freedom of movement: internal (right to move inside country) – Article 19; external (right to move out and come back) – Article 21

Freedom of Residence – right to reside (temporarily) and settle (permanently) in any part of country; removes internal barriers; promotes nationalism; reasonable restrictions on grounds of interest of general public and protection of interests of scheduled tribes; tribals permitted to regulate property rights according to customary rules
Supreme Court: certain areas can be banned for prostitutes and habitual offenders
Right to residence and right to movement are overlapping and complementary

Freedom of Profession, etc. – right to practice any profession, carry on any occupation, trade or business; covers all means of earning livelihood; reasonable restrictions in interest of general public
State can prescribe professional/technical qualifications
State can carry on any trade, business, industry or service to exclusion (complete or partial) of citizens or otherwise – no requirement to justify monopoly
Right does not include immoral (trafficking in women/children) or dangerous (harmful drugs/explosives) occupations – State can absolutely prohibit or regulate through licensing
Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences – Article 20
Article 20 grants protection against arbitrary and excessive punishment to accused person (citizen, foreigner, legal person)
Three provisions: No ex-post-facto law; No double jeopardy; No self-incrimination
Ex-post-facto law – law imposing penalties retrospectively – prohibited for criminal laws, not for civil or tax laws
First provision prohibits conviction or sentence under ex-post-facto criminal law, not trial; protection not available in preventive detention or demanding security

Double jeopardy – no person shall be prosecuted and punished for same offence more than once; available only in proceedings before court of law or judicial tribunal, not departmental or administrative authorities

Self-incrimination – no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself; extends to oral and documentary evidence; does not extend to compulsory production of material objects, thumb impression, specimen signature, blood specimens, compulsory exhibition of body; extends only to criminal proceedings, not civil or non-criminal
Protection of Life and Personal Liberty – Article 21
Article 21 declares no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law
Right available to both citizens and non-citizens

Gopalan case (1950) – narrow interpretation: protection only against arbitrary executive action, not legislative action; ‘procedure established by law’ different from ‘due process of law’; validity of law cannot be questioned on grounds of unreasonableness; ‘personal liberty’ means only liberty relating to person or body

Menaka case (1978) – overruled Gopalan; wider interpretation: procedure must be reasonable, fair, just; introduced ‘due process of law’ concept; protection against both executive and legislative action; ‘right to life’ includes right to live with human dignity and all aspects making life meaningful; ‘personal liberty’ of widest amplitude covering variety of rights
Rights declared as part of Article 21 (list of 35 rights)
Right to live with human dignity
Right to decent environment (pollution free water and air, protection against hazardous industries)
Right to livelihood
Right to privacy
Right to shelter
Right to health
Right to free education up to 14 years of age
Right to free legal aid
Right against solitary confinement
Right to speedy trial
Right against handcuffing
Right against inhuman treatment
Right against delayed execution
Right to travel abroad
Right against bonded labour
Right against custodial harassment
Right to emergency medical aid
Right to timely medical treatment in government hospital
Right not to be driven out of a state
Right to fair trial
Right of prisoner to have necessities of life
Right of women to be treated with decency and dignity
Right against public hanging
Right to road in hilly areas
Right to information
Right to reputation
Right of appeal from judgment of conviction
Right to family pension
Right to social and economic justice and empowerment
Right against bar fetters
Right to appropriate life insurance policy
Right to sleep
Right to freedom from noise pollution
Right to sustainable development
Right to opportunity
Right to Education – Article 21A
State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years
Makes only elementary education a Fundamental Right, not higher or professional
Added by 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 – described as ‘dawn of second revolution in citizens’ rights’
Before amendment, Article 45 in Part IV (Directive Principles) provided for free and compulsory education but not enforceable
Article 45 now changed: State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until age six
New fundamental duty under Article 51A: duty of every citizen to provide opportunities for education to child/ward between age six and fourteen
In 1993, Supreme Court recognised Fundamental Right to primary education under Article 21
Court held every child has right to free education until completing age 14; thereafter subject to economic capacity and development of state
Court overruled earlier judgment (1992) that there was fundamental right to education up to any level including professional
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 – enacted in pursuance of Article 21A
RTE Act: every child has right to full-time elementary education of satisfactory and equitable quality in formal school meeting essential norms and standards
Protection Against Arrest and Detention – Article 22
Two types of detention: punitive (after trial and conviction) and preventive (without trial, to prevent future offence, based on suspicion)
Article 22 has two parts: ordinary law and preventive detention law

First part – rights of person arrested under ordinary law: right to be informed of grounds of arrest; right to consult and be defended by legal practitioner; right to be produced before magistrate within 24 hours including journey time; right to be released after 24 hours unless magistrate authorises further detention
These safeguards not available to enemy alien or person arrested under preventive detention law

Supreme Court: first part does not cover arrest under court orders, civil arrest, arrest for failure to pay income tax, deportation of alien – applies only to criminal or quasi-criminal acts or activity prejudicial to public interest

Second part – protection for persons detained under preventive detention law: detention cannot exceed three months unless advisory board (of High Court judges) reports sufficient cause; grounds of detention communicated to detenu (but facts against public interest need not be disclosed); detenu afforded opportunity to make representation against detention order
Parliament can prescribe: circumstances/classes for detention beyond three months without advisory board opinion; maximum period of detention; procedure for advisory board inquiry
44th Amendment Act, 1978 reduced period without advisory board opinion from three to two months but not brought into force – original three months continues

Legislative power for preventive detention: Parliament exclusive for reasons connected with defence, foreign affairs, security of India; both Parliament and state legislatures concurrent for reasons connected with security of state, maintenance of public order, maintenance of supplies and services essential to community

Preventive detention laws enacted by Parliament: Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (expired 1969); Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971 (repealed 1978); Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA), 1974; National Security Act (NASA), 1980; Prevention of Blackmarketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act (PBMSECA), 1980; Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act (TADA), 1985 (repealed 1995); Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act (PITNDPSA), 1988; Prevention of Terrorism Act (POTA), 2002 (repealed 2004); Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, amended in 2004, 2008, 2012, 2019
No democratic country has made preventive detention integral part of Constitution as India; unknown in USA; Britain resorted only during WWI and WWII
Preventive detention existed during British rule: Bengal State Prisoners Regulation of 1818; Defence of India Act of 1939
Right against Exploitation – Article 23
Prohibition of traffic in human beings, begar (forced labour) and other similar forms of forced labour
Contravention is an offence punishable by law
Right available to both citizens and non-citizens
Protects individual against State and private persons
‘Traffic in human beings’ includes selling/buying men, women, children; immoral traffic including prostitution; devadasis; slavery
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 – to punish these acts
‘Begar’ means compulsory work without remuneration – Indian system under zamindars forcing tenants
‘Forced labour’ includes compelling person to work against will; ‘force’ includes physical/legal force and compulsion of economic circumstances (working for less than minimum wage)
Related laws: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976; Minimum Wages Act, 1948; Contract Labour Act, 1970; Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
Exception: State can impose compulsory service for public purposes (military or social service) without pay; but no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste or class
Prohibition of Employment of Children in Factories, etc. – Article 24
Prohibits employment of children below 14 years in any factory, mine or other hazardous activities (construction, railway)
Does not prohibit employment in harmless or innocent work
Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 – most important law

Other laws: Employment of Children Act, 1938; Factories Act, 1948; Mines Act, 1952; Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; Plantation Labour Act, 1951; Motor Transport Workers Act, 1951; Apprentices Act, 1961; Bidi and Cigar Workers Act, 1966; and other similar acts

1996 – Supreme Court directed establishment of Child Labour Rehabilitation Welfare Fund with offending employer depositing fine of ₹20,000 per child employed; directions for improvement of education, health, nutrition of children

Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 – established National Commission and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights and Children’s Courts for speedy trial of offences against children

2006 – government banned employment of children as domestic servants or workers in hotels, dhabas, restaurants, shops, factories, resorts, spas, tea-shops, etc.; warning of prosecution and penal action
Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 – amended 1986 Act; renamed as Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986
Right to Freedom of Religion – Articles 25-28
Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice and Propagation of Religion – Article 25
All persons equally entitled to freedom of conscience and right to freely profess, practice and propagate religion
Freedom of conscience – inner freedom to mould relation with God/Creatures
Right to profess – declaration of religious beliefs openly and freely
Right to practice – performance of worship, rituals, ceremonies, exhibition of beliefs
Right to propagate – transmission of religious beliefs to others; does not include right to convert; forcible conversions impinge on freedom of conscience
Article 25 covers both religious beliefs (doctrines) and religious practices (rituals)
Rights available to all persons – citizens and non-citizens
Subject to public order, morality, health and other fundamental rights provisions
State can regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice
State can provide for social welfare and reform or throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus
Explanations under Article 25: wearing and carrying of kirpans included in profession of Sikh religion; Hindus include Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists
Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs – Article 26

Every religious denomination or its section has rights: establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes; manage own affairs in matters of religion; own and acquire movable and immovable property; administer such property in accordance with law
Article 25 guarantees individual rights; Article 26 guarantees collective freedom of religion of denominations
Rights under Article 26 subject to public order, morality and health (not subject to other fundamental rights provisions)
Supreme Court conditions for religious denomination: collection of individuals with system of beliefs conducive to spiritual well-being; common organisation; distinctive name
Ramakrishna Mission and Ananda Marga held to be religious denominations within Hindu religion
Aurobindo Society not a religious denomination
Freedom from Taxation for Promotion of a Religion – Article 27
No person compelled to pay any taxes for promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination
State should not spend public money collected by tax for promotion of particular religion
Prohibits State from favouring, patronising, supporting one religion over another
Taxes can be used for promotion or maintenance of all religions
Prohibits levy of a tax, not a fee; fee can be levied on pilgrims for special services/safety measures; fee on religious endowments for regulation expenditure
Freedom from Attending Religious Instruction – Article 28
No religious instruction in educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds
Exception: institution administered by State but established under endowment or trust requiring imparting of religious instruction (permitted)
In institutions recognised by State or receiving aid, no person required to attend religious instruction or worship without consent; for minor, guardian's consent needed

Four types of institutions: (a) wholly maintained by State – religious instruction prohibited; (b) administered by State but established under endowment/trust – religious instruction permitted; (c) recognised by State; (d) receiving aid from State – (c) and (d) religious instruction permitted on voluntary basis
Cultural and Educational Rights – Articles 29-30
Protection of Interests of Minorities – Article 29
Any section of citizens residing in any part of India having distinct language, script or culture shall have right to conserve the same
No citizen denied admission into any educational institution maintained by State or receiving aid on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language
First provision protects group rights; second protects individual rights
Article 29 protects both religious and linguistic minorities
Supreme Court: scope not restricted to minorities – words 'section of citizens' include majority
Right to conserve language includes right to agitate for protection; political speeches/promises for conservation of language not corrupt practice under Representation of the People Act, 1951
Right of Minorities to Establish and Administer Educational Institutions – Article 30
All minorities (religious or linguistic) shall have right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice
Compensation amount fixed by State for compulsory acquisition of property of minority educational institution shall not restrict or abrogate right – added by 44th Amendment Act, 1978
In granting aid, State shall not discriminate against any educational institution managed by minority
Protection under Article 30 only for minorities (religious or linguistic), not any section of citizens as under Article 29
Term 'minority' not defined anywhere in Constitution
Right includes right to impart education to children in own language
Three types of minority educational institutions: (a) seeking recognition and aid; (b) seeking only recognition; (c) seeking neither recognition nor aid
Institutions of first and second type subject to State regulatory power for syllabus, academic standards, discipline, sanitation, employment of teaching staff, etc.
Institutions of third type free to administer affairs subject to general laws (contract, labour, industrial, tax, economic regulations)
Secretary of Malankara Syrian Catholic College case (2007) – Supreme Court summarised general principles

Principles: right includes choice of governing body, appointment of teaching/non-teaching staff, action for dereliction of duty, admission of eligible students, setting fee structure, use of properties
Right under Article 30 ensures equality with majority, not reverse discrimination; general laws apply equally
Right not absolute; does not include right to maladminister; regulatory measures for educational standards and academic excellence allowed
Regulations concerning welfare of students/teachers, eligibility criteria, qualifications, conditions of service, prevention of exploitation, syllabus/curriculum do not interfere with Article 30(1)
Unaided minority educational institutions have freedom to appoint teachers by rational procedure subject to eligibility/qualifications
Extension of aid does not alter nature; conditions can be imposed to ensure proper utilization without diluting right
Right to Constitutional Remedies – Article 32
Article 32 confers right to remedies for enforcement of fundamental rights – in itself a fundamental right
Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 most important article, 'the very soul and heart of the Constitution'
Supreme Court ruled Article 32 is a basic feature of Constitution – cannot be abridged or taken away even by amendment

Provisions of Article 32: (a) right to move Supreme Court for enforcement; (b) Supreme Court can issue directions/orders/writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto); (c) Parliament can empower any other court (excluding high courts as Article 226 already confers power) to issue writs; (d) right to move Supreme Court cannot be suspended except as provided (President can suspend during national emergency under Article 359)
Supreme Court is defender and guarantor of fundamental rights – vested with original and wide powers
Purpose of Article 32: guaranteed, effective, expeditious, inexpensive, summary remedy
Only fundamental rights can be enforced under Article 32, not other rights
Violation of a fundamental right is sine qua non for exercise of Article 32
Supreme Court under Article 32 cannot determine question not involving fundamental rights
Jurisdiction of Supreme Court under Article 32 is original but not exclusive – concurrent with high court under Article 226
High courts also have original powers under Article 226 to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights
Aggrieved party can move either high court or Supreme Court directly
Availability of alternate remedy is no bar to relief under Article 32 (since it is a fundamental right)
Supreme Court ruled where relief through high court available under Article 226, aggrieved party should first move high court
Writs – Types and Scope
Supreme Court (Article 32) and high courts (Article 226) can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto
Parliament (under Article 32) can empower any other court to issue these writs – no such provision made so far
Before 1950, only High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras could issue writs
Article 226 now empowers all high courts
Writs borrowed from English law – 'prerogative writs' issued in exercise of prerogative of King as fountain of justice

Writ jurisdiction of Supreme Court vs high court: (1) Supreme Court only for fundamental rights; high court for fundamental rights and any other purpose (enforcement of ordinary legal right) – narrower for Supreme Court; (2) Supreme Court territorial jurisdiction throughout India; high court limited to its territorial jurisdiction or where cause of action arises within – wider for Supreme Court; (3) Remedy under Article 32 is a fundamental right, court may not refuse; remedy under Article 226 is discretionary, high court may refuse

Habeas Corpus – Latin 'to have the body'; order to person detaining another to produce body before court; court examines cause and legality; sets free if illegal; bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention
Habeas corpus can be issued against public authorities and private individuals
Not issued where detention lawful, proceeding for contempt of legislature/court, detention by competent court, detention outside court's jurisdiction
Mandamus – Latin 'we command'; command to public official to perform official duties failed or refused; can be issued against public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal, government

Mandamus cannot be issued against private individual/body; to enforce departmental instruction without statutory force; when duty discretionary not mandatory; to enforce contractual obligation; against President of India or state governors; against Chief Justice of High Court acting in judicial capacity

Prohibition – Latin 'to forbid'; higher court to lower court/tribunal to prevent exceeding jurisdiction or usurping jurisdiction; directs inactivity; can be issued only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities, not administrative, legislative, private individuals

Certiorari – Latin 'to be certified'; higher court to lower court/tribunal to transfer pending case to itself or to squash order; grounds: excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction, error of law; both preventive and curative; earlier only against judicial/quasi-judicial; 1991 Supreme Court ruled can be issued even against administrative authorities affecting rights; not available against legislative bodies and private individuals

Quo-Warranto – Latin 'by what authority or warrant'; court enquires into legality of claim of person to public office; prevents illegal usurpation; can be issued only for substantive public office of permanent character created by statute or Constitution; not for ministerial or private office; can be sought by any interested person, not necessarily aggrieved person
Armed Forces and Fundamental Rights – Article 33
Parliament can restrict or abrogate fundamental rights of members of armed forces, para-military forces, police forces, intelligence agencies and analogous forces
Objective: ensure proper discharge of duties and maintenance of discipline
Power to make laws under Article 33 conferred only on Parliament, not state legislatures
Such law cannot be challenged in any court on ground of contravention of fundamental rights
Laws enacted: Army Act (1950), Navy Act (1950), Air Force Act (1950), Police Forces (Restriction of Rights) Act, 1966, Border Security Force Act, etc.

These impose restrictions on freedom of speech, right to form associations, right to be members of trade unions/political associations, right to communicate with press, right to attend public meetings/demonstrations
Expression 'members of armed forces' also covers non-combatant employees (barbers, carpenters, mechanics, cooks, chowkidars, bootmakers, tailors)
Parliamentary law under Article 33 can exclude court martial from writ jurisdiction of Supreme Court and high courts for enforcement of fundamental rights
Martial Law and Fundamental Rights – Article 34
Article 34 provides for restrictions on fundamental rights while martial law in force
Parliament can indemnify any government servant or other person for acts done in connection with maintenance/restoration of order where martial law was in force
Parliament can validate any sentence passed, punishment inflicted, forfeiture ordered or other act done under martial law
Act of Indemnity cannot be challenged in any court on ground of contravention of fundamental rights
Concept of martial law borrowed from English common law

Expression 'martial law' not defined in Constitution – literally 'military rule'; civil administration run by military authorities under their own rules outside ordinary law; implies suspension of ordinary law and government by military tribunals
Different from military law applicable to armed forces
No specific provision authorising executive to declare martial law – implicit in Article 34
Martial law imposed under extraordinary circumstances: war, invasion, insurrection, rebellion, riot, violent resistance to law – justification to repel force to maintain/restore order
During martial law, military authorities vested with abnormal powers – impose restrictions on civilians, punish, even condemn to death
Supreme Court: declaration of martial law does not ipso facto result in suspension of writ of habeas corpus
Differences between Martial Law and National Emergency (Table 7.3)
Martial law affects only Fundamental Rights; National Emergency affects Centre-state relations, distribution of revenues, legislative powers, may extend tenure of Parliament
Martial law suspends government and ordinary law courts; National Emergency continues them
Martial law imposed to restore breakdown of law and order; National Emergency on three grounds: war, external aggression, armed rebellion
Martial law imposed in specific area; National Emergency in whole country or any part
Martial law has no specific provision in Constitution (implicit); National Emergency has specific/detailed provisions (explicit)
Effecting Certain Fundamental Rights – Article 35
Power to make laws to give effect to certain specified fundamental rights vests only in Parliament, not state legislatures – ensures uniformity throughout India

Parliament (and not state legislature) shall have power to make laws with respect to: prescribing residence as condition for employment (Article 16); empowering courts other than Supreme Court and high courts to issue writs for enforcement (Article 32); restricting/abrogating fundamental rights to armed forces etc. (Article 33); indemnifying persons for acts during martial law (Article 34)

Parliament shall have power to make laws for prescribing punishment for acts declared offences under fundamental rights: untouchability (Article 17); traffic in human beings and forced labour (Article 23)
Parliament shall after commencement of Constitution make laws for prescribing punishment for these acts – obligatory
Any law in force at commencement with respect to these matters continues until altered/repealed/amended by Parliament
Article 35 extends competence of Parliament even if matters fall within State List
Present Position of Right to Property
Originally right to property under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 – one of seven fundamental rights
Article 19(1)(f) guaranteed right to acquire, hold, dispose of property

Article 31 guaranteed right against deprivation of property; provided no deprivation except by authority of law; empowered State to acquire/requisition property for public purpose and on payment of compensation
Most controversial fundamental right – caused confrontations between Supreme Court and Parliament
Led to several constitutional amendments: 1st, 4th, 7th, 25th, 39th, 40th, 42nd – added/modified Articles 31A, 31B, 31C to nullify effects of court judgments

44th Amendment Act, 1978 abolished right to property as fundamental right – repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31; inserted new Article 300A in Part XII – no person deprived of property except by authority of law
Right to property now a legal/constitutional right, not fundamental right; not part of basic structure

Implications: can be regulated by ordinary law without constitutional amendment; protects against executive action but not legislative action; aggrieved person cannot move Supreme Court under Article 32; can move High Court under Article 226; no guaranteed right to compensation for acquisition/requisition

Two cases where compensation still guaranteed: when State acquires property of minority educational institution (Article 30); when State acquires land held under personal cultivation within statutory ceiling (Article 31A)
First provision added by 44th Amendment Act (1978); second by 17th Amendment Act (1964)
Articles 31A, 31B, 31C retained as exceptions to fundamental rights
Exceptions to Fundamental Rights
Saving of Laws Providing for Acquisition of Estates, etc. – Article 31A

Article 31A saves five categories of laws from being challenged on ground of contravention of Articles 14 and 19: (a) acquisition of estates and related rights; (b) taking over management of properties; (c) amalgamation of corporations; (d) extinguishment/modification of rights of directors/shareholders; (e) extinguishment/modification of mining leases
Article 31A does not immunise state law from judicial review unless reserved for President's consideration and assented
Article 31A provides for payment of compensation at market value when State acquires land held under personal cultivation within statutory ceiling
Validation of Certain Acts and Regulations – Article 31B
Article 31B saves acts and regulations included in Ninth Schedule from being challenged on ground of contravention of any fundamental rights
Scope wider than Article 31A – immunises any law in Ninth Schedule from all fundamental rights

I.R. Coelho case (2007) – Supreme Court ruled no blanket immunity from judicial review for Ninth Schedule laws; judicial review is a basic feature; laws placed after April 24, 1973 open to challenge if they violate Articles 14, 15, 19, 21 or basic structure
April 24, 1973 – date of Kesavananda Bharati case where basic structure doctrine propounded
Originally Ninth Schedule contained 13 acts and regulations (1951); at present (2016) number is 282 – include land reforms, abolition of zamindari system, other matters
Saving of Laws Giving Effect to Certain Directive Principles – Article 31C

Article 31C inserted by 25th Amendment Act, 1971 – two provisions: (a) no law implementing socialistic directive principles of Article 39(b) or (c) shall be void for contravention of Article 14 or 19; (b) no law containing declaration that it gives effect to such policy shall be questioned in court
Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) – Supreme Court declared second provision unconstitutional as judicial review is basic feature
First provision held constitutional and valid
42nd Amendment Act (1976) extended scope of first provision to include any law implementing any directive principle in Part IV – declared unconstitutional in Minerva Mills case (1980)
Criticism of Fundamental Rights

Excessive limitations – subjected to innumerable exceptions, restrictions, qualifications, explanations; critics: Constitution grants rights with one hand and takes away with the other; Jaspat Roy Kapoor suggested renaming as 'Limitations on Fundamental Rights' or 'Fundamental Rights and Limitations Thereon'

No social and economic rights – list mainly political rights; no provision for right to social security, right to work, right to employment, right to rest and leisure – these available in advanced democracies and erstwhile USSR/China

No clarity – stated in vague, indefinite, ambiguous manner; phrases like 'public order', 'minorities', 'reasonable restriction', 'public interest' not clearly defined; language complicated; Sir Ivor Jennings called Constitution of India a 'paradise for lawyers'
No permanency – Parliament can curtail or abolish (e.g., right to property in 1978); 'doctrine of basic structure' only limitation
Suspension during Emergency – enforcement suspended during National Emergency (except Articles 20 and 21); critics: rights should be enjoyable in all situations
Expensive remedy – judicial process too expensive for common man; rights benefit mainly rich section

Preventive detention – Article 22 takes away spirit and substance; confers arbitrary powers on State; negates individual liberty; no democratic country has made preventive detention integral part of Constitution as India
No consistent philosophy – chapter not product of philosophical principle; Sir Ivor Jennings: Fundamental Rights based on no consistent philosophy; creates difficulty for courts in interpretation
Significance of Fundamental Rights
Constitute bedrock of democratic system
Provide necessary conditions for material and moral protection of man
Serve as formidable bulwark of individual liberty
Facilitate establishment of rule of law
Protect interests of minorities and weaker sections
Strengthen secular fabric of Indian State
Check absoluteness of authority of government
Lay foundation stone of social equality and social justice
Ensure dignity and respect of individuals
Facilitate participation of people in political and administrative process
Rights Outside Part III
Constitutional rights/legal rights/non-fundamental rights in other parts
No tax levied except by authority of law – Article 265 (Part XII)
No person deprived of property save by authority of law – Article 300-A (Part XII)
Trade, commerce and intercourse throughout territory of India free – Article 301 (Part XIII)
These are justiciable but different from Fundamental Rights
In case of violation of Fundamental Right, aggrieved person can move Supreme Court under Article 32 (fundamental right itself)
In case of violation of these rights, cannot avail Article 32; can move High Court by ordinary suit or under Article 226
